title: Hydrogen
tagline: The lightest element, its isotopes, its unique position in the periodic table, its preparation and properties, its compounds with oxygen and with metals, and the chemistry of water and hydrogen peroxide.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Chemistry syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Chemistry registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question. The official CISCE ISC Class XI Chemistry syllabus treats Hydrogen as a prescribed inorganic chapter, so the content follows that syllabus framing.

overview.intro: Hydrogen is the simplest element, but it is not a simple topic. It has a place of its own in the periodic table because its properties are unlike those of any single group. It also shows important chemistry in its own right: it forms compounds such as water and hydrogen chloride, it can behave like a metal or a non-metal depending on conditions, and its heavier isotope deuterium has its own uses. This chapter gives hydrogen its due as an element and as a starting point for understanding several other important compounds.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Position in the periodic table; isotopes; dihydrogen; preparation and properties of H2; hydrides; water; heavy water; hydrogen peroxide; hydrogen as a fuel

learningOutcomes: Explain why hydrogen occupies a special position in the periodic table.
Describe the isotopes of hydrogen and their differences.
Describe the preparation and properties of dihydrogen.
Distinguish between ionic, covalent and metallic hydrides.
Explain the structure and properties of water and heavy water.
Describe the chemistry of hydrogen peroxide.
Discuss the uses of hydrogen and its potential as a fuel.
Avoid the misconception that hydrogen always behaves like an alkali metal or always like a halogen.

blocks.text: Hydrogen is placed first in the periodic table because it has the simplest atom, with one proton and one electron. But its chemistry does not fit perfectly into any one group. It can lose an electron to form H+, like alkali metals, and it can gain an electron to form H-, like halogens. It can also form covalent bonds. This dual character is why hydrogen is often treated separately. The useful point is not to force hydrogen into a single family, but to recognize that it has some alkali-metal-like and some halogen-like properties, yet is ultimately its own case.

items: Hydrogen has one electron and one proton.
It can behave like an alkali metal by losing an electron.
It can behave like a halogen by gaining an electron.
It also forms covalent bonds.
Its position is special, not completely typical of any group.

items.text: In water, hydrogen is covalently bonded to oxygen. In sodium hydride, hydrogen is present as H-, more like a halide ion. The same element can appear very differently depending on the compound.
items.note: The example shows why hydrogen is not easily reduced to a single group behavior.

blocks.text: Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium, deuterium and tritium. They all have one proton, but they differ in the number of neutrons. Protium is the most common isotope and has no neutron. Deuterium has one neutron and is sometimes called heavy hydrogen. Tritium has two neutrons and is radioactive. The chemical properties of isotopes are very similar, but their masses differ, so physical properties and rates of reactions can differ. In some cases, deuterium is used as a label to trace chemical reactions.

items: Protium has no neutron.
Deuterium has one neutron.
Tritium has two neutrons and is radioactive.
Isotopes have similar chemistry but different masses.
Deuterium is useful in tracing and in heavy water.

items.text: Heavy water, D2O, contains deuterium instead of ordinary hydrogen. It is chemically similar to ordinary water but has a higher mass, which changes some physical properties and makes it useful in certain applications.
items.note: The example brings the isotope idea into a familiar compound.

blocks.text: Dihydrogen is the common form of hydrogen gas, H2. It is a colorless, odorless gas with low density. It can be prepared in the laboratory by reactions that release hydrogen, such as the reaction of certain metals with acids. It is also produced by other methods on a larger scale. In chemical reactions, hydrogen can combine with many elements and can also act as a reducing agent. These properties make it important in industry and in the laboratory.

items: Dihydrogen is H2 gas.
It is colorless, odorless and lighter than air.
It can be prepared by reactions of metals with acids.
It can act as a reducing agent.
It burns in air to form water.

items.text: Zinc reacting with dilute acid is a common laboratory way to produce hydrogen gas. The gas can be collected and tested by its burning behavior.
items.note: The example connects a familiar laboratory preparation with the properties of hydrogen.

blocks.text: Hydrides are compounds of hydrogen with other elements. They can be broadly classified into ionic hydrides, covalent hydrides and metallic hydrides. Ionic hydrides are formed with electropositive metals and contain the hydride ion H-. Covalent hydrides are formed with many non-metals and include compounds such as methane and water. Metallic hydrides are formed with some metals and can store hydrogen in the metal lattice. The classification helps explain why hydrogen compounds can be so different in properties.

items: Ionic hydrides contain H- and are formed with some electropositive metals.
Covalent hydrides are formed with non-metals.
Metallic hydrides involve hydrogen in a metal lattice.
The type of hydride depends on the element hydrogen is combined with.
Hydrides range from reactive salts to familiar molecules.

items.text: Sodium hydride is an ionic hydride and reacts with water to release hydrogen. Methane is a covalent hydride. The two behave very differently because of the nature of the bonding.
items.note: The example contrasts two hydrides to make the classification meaningful.

blocks.text: Water is one of the most important compounds of hydrogen and oxygen. Its structure is bent, and it has hydrogen bonding, which gives it unusual properties such as a high boiling point and good solvent behavior for many substances. Heavy water is the deuterated form, D2O, and resembles ordinary water in many ways but differs in mass and in some physical properties. Heavy water is used in some nuclear reactors and in research. A student should remember that the special properties of water are not accidental; they come from its structure and hydrogen bonding.

items: Water has a bent molecular structure.
Hydrogen bonding affects its properties.
Water is a good solvent for many substances.
Heavy water is D2O with deuterium.
Heavy water has different physical properties from ordinary water.

items.text: Ice floats on water because water expands on freezing due to hydrogen bonding. This is a familiar but important fact that reflects the structure of water.
items.note: The example connects structure to a well-known property.

blocks.text: Hydrogen peroxide, H2O2, is a pale blue liquid in pure form and a common oxidizing agent. It can decompose to water and oxygen, and this decomposition can be catalyzed by light, heat or impurities. Hydrogen peroxide has uses as a disinfectant, bleach and oxidizing agent. Its chemistry is useful to study because it shows how a compound can act as an oxidant and how its stability depends on conditions. It is also an example of a compound with an O-O bond.

items: Hydrogen peroxide is H2O2.
It is an oxidizing agent.
It can decompose to water and oxygen.
It has an O-O bond.
It has uses as a disinfectant and bleach.

items.text: When hydrogen peroxide decomposes, it releases oxygen. The decomposition can be slow in a clean bottle but faster if a catalyst or impurity is present.
items.note: The example explains why hydrogen peroxide requires careful storage.

blocks.text: Hydrogen has many uses. It is used in the manufacture of ammonia, in the hydrogenation of oils, in rocket propellants and in other industrial processes. It is also discussed as a possible fuel because its combustion produces only water. At the same time, hydrogen has practical difficulties: it is a gas with low density, it can escape easily, and producing it cleanly is a major challenge. The important idea is that hydrogen's usefulness is linked to both its chemical properties and the practical problems of handling it.

items: Hydrogen is used in ammonia manufacture and hydrogenation.
It is used in some propulsion and industrial applications.
Its combustion produces water.
Storage and handling are practical challenges.
Its fuel potential depends on how it is produced and used.

items.text: Hydrogen can be a clean-burning fuel in the sense that water is the main combustion product, but the overall environmental picture depends on how the hydrogen is made and stored.
items.note: The example avoids naive overstatement about hydrogen as a fuel.

keyPoints: Hydrogen has a special position in the periodic table.
It can show alkali-metal-like and halogen-like behavior.
The three isotopes are protium, deuterium and tritium.
Dihydrogen is H2 gas and can act as a reducing agent.
Hydrides can be ionic, covalent or metallic.
Water's properties arise from its structure and hydrogen bonding.
Heavy water is D2O and differs from ordinary water in mass.
Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidizing agent with an O-O bond.
Hydrogen has important uses but also practical handling challenges.
examFocus: Do not treat hydrogen as belonging fully to one group.
Remember that isotopes differ in mass, not in chemical identity.
Distinguish among ionic, covalent and metallic hydrides.
Explain water's properties with reference to hydrogen bonding.
Do not confuse hydrogen peroxide with water.

vocabulary.meaning: Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The most common isotope of hydrogen, with no neutron.
The hydrogen isotope with one neutron.
The hydrogen isotope with two neutrons; radioactive.
A compound of hydrogen with another element.
A pale blue oxidizing agent with formula H2O2.
A substance that can reduce another substance, often by providing electrons or hydrogen.

questions.prompt: The atomic number of hydrogen is:
The common isotopes of hydrogen are:
questions.explanation: Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium, deuterium and tritium.
questions.commonMistake: Adding unrelated elements to the list of isotopes.

questions.prompt: Which isotope of hydrogen is radioactive?
questions.explanation: Tritium is radioactive; protium and deuterium are not.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking all hydrogen isotopes are radioactive.

questions.prompt: Hydrogen can behave like a halogen by:
options: Losing an electron to form H+
Gaining an electron to form H-
questions.answer: Gaining an electron to form H-
questions.explanation: Hydrogen can gain an electron like halogens, forming H-.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking hydrogen only behaves like an alkali metal.

options: A solid with a strong color
questions.explanation: H2 is colorless, odorless and light.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking hydrogen is a heavy gas.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a covalent hydride?

questions.explanation: Heavy water is D2O, water made with deuterium.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing heavy water with hydrogen peroxide.

questions.prompt: Hydrogen peroxide acts mainly as a:
questions.explanation: Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidizing agent.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking H2O2 is chemically identical to water.

questions.prompt: Why does hydrogen have a special position in the periodic table?
options: Because it belongs fully to Group 1 only
Because it has properties similar to both alkali metals and halogens
Because it is a liquid at room temperature
questions.answer: Because it has properties similar to both alkali metals and halogens
questions.explanation: Hydrogen shows some alkali-metal-like and some halogen-like properties.
questions.commonMistake: Forcing hydrogen fully into one group.

questions.prompt: Which statement about isotopes is correct?
options: They have different numbers of protons
They have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
questions.answer: They have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
questions.explanation: Isotopes differ in neutron number, not proton number.

questions.prompt: Why is hydrogen placed separately in many discussions of the periodic table?
questions.answer: Because it has some properties like alkali metals and some like halogens, so it does not fit perfectly into one group.
questions.explanation: Hydrogen's dual character justifies its special treatment.
questions.commonMistake: Saying hydrogen belongs to only one group.

questions.answer: Heavy water is water in which deuterium replaces ordinary hydrogen, giving D2O.
questions.explanation: Heavy water contains deuterium instead of ordinary hydrogen.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing heavy water with hydrogen peroxide.

questions.prompt: State one important use of hydrogen.
questions.answer: Hydrogen is used in the manufacture of ammonia and in hydrogenation of oils.
questions.commonMistake: Saying hydrogen is only used as a laboratory gas.

questions.prompt: Which hydride contains the hydride ion H-?
questions.explanation: NaH is an ionic hydride containing H-.

questions.prompt: Which statement about hydrogen as a fuel is most accurate?
options: It burns to give only water, but storage and production are practical issues
It is always easy to store and use anywhere
It burns to give carbon dioxide only
questions.answer: It burns to give only water, but storage and production are practical issues
questions.explanation: Hydrogen's combustion product is water, but handling and production are challenging.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking hydrogen is an effortless perfect fuel in every respect.
